# If This Was a Movie (Taylor Swift song)
"If This Was a Movie" is a song by American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift. It was released as a bonus track on the deluxe edition of Swift’s third studio album, Speak Now (2010). Swift co-wrote the song with Martin Johnson (lead singer of Boys Like Girls), making it the only track on Speak Now (deluxe) that was not written solely by Swift. Musically, “If This Was a Movie” is a pop rock-leaning ballad about longing for an ex-lover to return, using the metaphor of a cinematic reunion. Critics noted that the song marked Swift’s transition toward more mature themes of heartbreak, moving beyond the high school fairy-tale imagery of her earlier work. Billboard magazine gave the track a positive review, rating it 4 out of 5 stars and describing it as “a more age-appropriate” step for Swift’s then-innocent country image.
## Background and Release
“If This Was a Movie” was recorded during the Speak Now sessions and included as one of three bonus tracks on the Target-exclusive deluxe edition of the album (alongside “Ours” and “Superman”). Unlike the standard Speak Now tracks, which Swift wrote entirely on her own, this song was co-written with Martin Johnson. Swift and Johnson had previously collaborated on the Boys Like Girls song “Two Is Better Than One” (2009) and the Hannah Montana: The Movie soundtrack song “You’ll Always Find Your Way Back Home”. The inclusion of a co-writer made “If This Was a Movie” unique on Speak Now’s deluxe edition.
Initially, the song was only available with physical copies of Speak Now (Deluxe) sold at Target stores in 2010. On November 8, 2011, Big Machine Records released “If This Was a Movie” (along with the other deluxe tracks) as a digital single via iTunes and Amazon. It was issued as a promotional single to promote the Speak Now album’s deluxe content, while “Ours” was serviced to country radio as the next official single. Upon its digital release, “If This Was a Movie” sold approximately 162,000 downloads in its first week. This strong sales debut propelled the song onto the charts: it entered the US Billboard Hot 100 at number 10 on the chart dated November 26, 2011. At the time, this made Swift the first artist to score eight Hot 100 debuts in the top ten. The song also reached number 17 on the Canadian Hot 100 in that frame. In the United Kingdom, where it was not actively promoted, “If This Was a Movie” charted at a modest No. 191 on the UK Singles Chart based on imports and downloads.
## Composition and Lyrics
Running 3 minutes and 54 seconds, “If This Was a Movie” is a midtempo ballad blending Swift’s country-pop style with pop rock elements. It is set to a simple, recurring guitar riff that drives the melody, with a gradual build into a dramatic chorus backed by subtle harmonies. Swift’s vocals carry a slight country twang, a signature of her early work, yet the song’s production leans toward polished pop rock. Lyrically, the track finds Swift daydreaming about a lost love coming back “like in the movies.” She imagines that if her heartbreak were a movie, there would be a climactic reunion – singing in the chorus, “Come back, come back, come back to me like you would if this was a movie… But if this was a movie, you’d be here by now.” In the verses, the then-20-year-old Swift expresses regret and nostalgia for a relationship that ended about six months prior. According to Billboard, the song suggests Swift “had been through a breakup and wishes to reverse it,” showcasing a more mature perspective compared to the high-school romance themes of her earlier hits. Critics observed that by abandoning fairy-tale endings and acknowledging real-world heartbreak, Swift was “lyrically coming of age” on this track. The title and concept play on Hollywood tropes – if life were like a movie, the estranged lover would dramatically return in the rain to apologize, giving the story a happy ending. This wistful narrative resonated with fans for its earnest portrayal of yearning and vulnerability.
## Critical Reception
Upon release, “If This Was a Movie” received generally positive reviews from music critics, especially considering its status as a bonus track. Billboard reviewers praised the song’s relatable storytelling and catchy melody. In Billboard’s track review, it was highlighted that Swift delivered the emotional narrative with a sense of innocence giving way to growth, and they rated the song 4 out of 5 stars. The review noted the song’s “age-appropriate” approach, meaning it showed Swift evolving beyond teenage fairy tales into more adult heartbreak themes. Although “If This Was a Movie” was not pushed as an official radio single, many fans and critics considered it a strong piece of the Speak Now deluxe collection. Taste of Country’s ranking of Speak Now tracks commented that while the song isn’t as immediately memorable as some of Swift’s singles, it exemplifies her gift for wistful, narrative songwriting at its best. The instrumentation and Swift’s heartfelt delivery were also well-regarded; Molly Trust of Billboard (in a retrospective piece) described the track as “corny but smart,” capturing an entire romantic drama in just a few minutes. Overall, reviewers appreciated that the bonus track maintained the high quality of Swift’s writing on Speak Now, rather than feeling like a throwaway.
On the other hand, because it was a late addition to the album, “If This Was a Movie” did not receive as much individual attention as Swift’s singles. Some critics noted that it might not have had the same impact or memorability as hits like “Back to December” or “Mean,” but it nonetheless holds a special place for fans who relate to its cinematic heartbreak scenario. As of 2018, Swift had never performed the song live, making it something of a deep-cut favorite. (Swift eventually gave the song its live debut as a surprise acoustic performance during her Eras Tour in June 2023, to the delight of longtime fans.)
## Commercial Performance
Without an official radio release, “If This Was a Movie” charted purely on the strength of digital sales. In the United States, the song’s first-week download sales (~162,000) led to its No. 10 debut on the Billboard Hot 100. It also debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard Digital Song Sales chart that week, indicating one of the highest digital sales totals in Swift’s career up to that point. The strong digital demand was fueled by fans who had waited a year for the deluxe tracks to become available outside of the Target CD. “If This Was a Movie” additionally topped Billboard’s Country Digital Song Sales chart upon release. This made Swift one of the few country artists at the time to have multiple songs (including deluxe tracks) reach No. 1 on that digital sales chart. In Canada, the song reached number 17 on the Canadian Hot 100, reflecting similar digital popularity north of the border. It spent a total of 12 weeks on the Hot 100 and also appeared on year-end charts for digital country songs. In international markets, “If This Was a Movie” had a more subdued impact. It did not chart in most major markets like Australia or Europe (since it wasn’t a formal single), though it did appear on the UK Singles Chart at No. 191 based on import sales and downloads.
By the end of the Speak Now era, “If This Was a Movie” had sold over half a million copies in the U.S., demonstrating longevity as a fan-favorite deep cut (its sales contributed to Swift’s total of 545,000 digital tracks sold in the week of its debut, which included other deluxe songs). Its Hot 100 peak at #10 was especially notable because Swift achieved that without any radio play or music video for the song. This feat underscored her strong fanbase and the commercial appeal of even her non-single tracks.
## Taylor’s Version Re-recording
In 2019, after a high-profile dispute over the ownership of her early master recordings, Taylor Swift began re-recording her back catalog. “If This Was a Movie” was among the songs Swift chose to re-record to regain control of her music. On March 17, 2023, Swift released “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)” as a standalone digital single, coinciding with the opening night of her Eras Tour. The re-recording was part of a special four-song release that day, which also included two other re-recorded tracks (“Eyes Open (Taylor’s Version)” and “Safe & Sound (Taylor’s Version)”) and one previously unreleased song from her vault (“All of the Girls You Loved Before”). Notably, Swift opted to include “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)” on an extended play titled The More Fearless (Taylor’s Version) Chapter – aligning it with her Fearless-era re-recordings – rather than on the Speak Now (Taylor’s Version) album. This decision was intentional: because the original song was co-written with Johnson, Swift kept it off the Speak Now (Taylor’s Version) tracklist in order to maintain the promise that Speak Now would remain an “entirely self-written” re-recorded album. By releasing the song earlier under the Fearless banner, Swift “tied up” that loose end and preserved the artistic narrative of Speak Now as solely her writing.
Musically, “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)” stays faithful to the 2010 arrangement, though Swift’s vocals – matured by over a decade – are noticeably richer and more controlled. Subtle production updates include a slightly more polished mix and re-recorded instrumental parts by Swift’s touring band members. Critics noted that Swift’s voice on the 2023 version sounds deeper and more resonant, which some felt added emotional weight, while others missed the youthful earnestness of the original recording. The Times’ critic Will Hodgkinson described the re-recorded song as “straightforward, innocent, slightly breathy balladry with an orchestral backing,” commenting that it retained the “corny but smart” charm of the original.
Upon release, “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)” achieved moderate commercial success. In the U.S., it did not enter the main Hot 100 (largely due to limited streaming compared to new singles), but it debuted at number 2 on Billboard’s Bubbling Under Hot 100 chart (effectively the equivalent of No. 102) and at number 4 on the Digital Song Sales chart with 11,300 copies sold in its release week. Impressively, the Taylor’s Version reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Country Digital Song Sales chart. Since the original 2011 version had also hit No. 1 on that chart in the past, Swift achieved a rare feat: “If This Was a Movie” became the first song to top the Country Digital Song Sales chart with two different recordings of the same composition. Internationally, the re-recorded song charted in a few markets driven by Swift’s fan interest. It made the top 10 of the digital sales charts in Canada and the United Kingdom, and reached No. 12 on New Zealand’s Hot Singles chart (a component ranking for new entries). These placements reflected the enthusiasm of fans, especially those completing their collections of Swift’s Taylor’s Version releases.
In reviews of the March 2023 batch of songs, “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)” was met with nostalgia and approval. Critics like Januar Aguja of The Freeman praised Swift’s matured vocals, suggesting that the new rendition could win over a fresh generation of listeners. Longtime fans appreciated that the re-recording stayed true to the spirit of the original track, while also fitting seamlessly into Swift’s ongoing project of reclaiming her music. With the Taylor’s Version available, Swift has ensured that future licensing and streaming of “If This Was a Movie” will benefit her directly, rather than the owners of her old masters – a key goal of her re-recordings.

![Image 1: "Speak Now" Prologue (Taylor Swift, 2010)](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=361x1024:format=jpg/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/ie87c76cbea1da317/version/1549742566/speak-now-prologue-taylor-swift-2010.jpg)

**"Speak now or forever hold your peace", the words said by the preachers at the end of wedding ceremonies all over the world, right before the vows. It's a last chance for protest, a moment that makes everyone's heart race, and a moment I've always been strangely fascinated by. So many fantasize about bursting into a church, saying what they'd kept inside for years like in the movies. In real life, it rarely happens.**

Real life is a funny thing, you know. In real life, saying the right thing at the right moment is beyond crucial. So crucial, in fact, that most of us start to hesitate, for fear of saying the wrong thing at the wrong time. But lately what I've begun to fear more than that is letting that moment pass without saying anything. I think most of us fear reaching the end of our life, and looking back regretting the moments we didn't speak up. When we didn't say **"I love you"**. When we should've said **"I'm sorry"**. When we didn't stand up for ourselves or someone who needed help.

These songs are made up of words I didn't say when the moment was right in front of me. **These songs are open letters.** Each is written with a specific person in mind, telling them what I meant to tell them in person. To the beautiful boy whose heart I broke in December. To my first love who I never thought would be my first heartbreak. To my band. To a mean man I used to be afraid of. To someone who made my world dark for a while. To a girl who stole something of mine. To someone I forgive for what he said in front of the whole world.

Words can break someone into a million pieces, but they can also put them back together. I hope you use yours for good, because the only words you'll regret more than the ones left unsaid are the ones that you use to intentionally hurt someone. What you say might be too much for some people. Maybe it will come out all wrong and you'll stutter and you'll walk away embarrassed, wincing as you play it all back in your head. But I think the words you stop yourself from saying are the ones that will haunt you the longest. So say it to them. Or say it to yourself in the mirror. Say it in a letter you'll never send or in a book millions might read someday. I think you deserve to look back on your life without a chorus of resounding voices saying **"I could've, but it's too late now"**.

There is a time for silence. There is a time waiting your turn. But if you know how you feel, and you clearly know what you need to say, you'll know it. **I don't think you should wait, I think you should speak now.**

Love, Taylor. ("Speak Now" Prologue)

PS: To all the boys who inspired this album, you should've known. 😉

![Image 2: Mine (Big Machine Records, 2010)](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=299x1024:format=png/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/i3485f12110c797fe/version/1535848517/mine-big-machine-records-2010.png)

**The album's lead single "Mine" tells the story of a girl whose parents' failed marriage has caused her to take a pessimistic view on love. Over time, however, she falls in love with someone who convinces her to start believing in love again.**

Taylor was inspired to write "Mine" after reflecting on one of her unnamed crushes and explained that the song is about her tendency to run from love. The song contains elements of power-pop and its lyrics speak of the ups and downs of a young love.

"This is a situation where a guy that I just barely knew put his arm around me by the water, and I saw the entire relationship flash before my eyes, almost like a weird science-fiction movie. After I wrote the song, things sort of fell apart, as things so often do. And I hadn’t talked to him in a couple months. And the song came out, and that day, I got an e-mail from him. And I was like, ‘Yes!’ Because that one was sort of half-confession and half-prediction or projection of what I saw." -- Taylor Swift

The song was released as the lead single from "[Speak Now](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/speak-now/the-album/ "The Album")". Following an unauthorized internet leak, the song was released on August 4, 2010, two weeks earlier than the intended release date.

Critical reception for "Mine" was mostly positive. Taylor was praised for her ability to show a mature perspective on love, although some critics called the song "formulaic" for resonating her earlier works, notably "Love Story".

The song was commercially successful, as well; it became a top ten hit in Australia, Canada and Japan. In the United States, the song entered the Billboard Hot 100 at number three, making Taylor the second female artist in the history of the Hot 100 to debut multiple tracks in the top five during a calendar year after Mariah Carey did so in 1995.

The song's accompanying music video was directed by Roman White. It chronicles the romantic relationship between Taylor and her love interest played by British actor Toby Hemingway which ends with a marriage. The music video was met with great praise from contemporary critics who deemed it as "rather sweet," and "heartwarming." It received the coveted "Video of the Year Award" at the CMT Music Awards 2011.

![Image 3](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=102x10000:format=png/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/i4e2ae67981e5173a/version/1548530989/image.png)

  

![Image 4: Sparks Fly (Big Machine Records, 2011)](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=299x1024:format=jpg/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/i2be1e055ba902073/version/1535849159/sparks-fly-big-machine-records-2011.jpg)

**"Sparks Fly" is a song Taylor wrote about falling for someone, despite knowing that she shouldn't -- but she can't deny the immediate connection.**

Taylor wrote the song when she was 16 years old, prior to the release of her debut single "[Tim McGraw](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/taylor-swift/the-songs/ "The Singles")" in 2006, after playing with her crush Jake Owen in a bar in Portland, Oregon. Following a 2007 live performance of the song, "Sparks Fly" grew in popularity among Taylor's fanbase. While "Speak Now" was under production, she received requests from fans to include the song on the album. As reported by _Taste of Country_, Taylor said:

"The song ‘Sparks Fly’ is about falling for someone that you maybe shouldn’t fall for, but you can‘t stop yourself because there’s such a connection, there’s such chemistry. This is a song that I wrote a few years ago and had been working on it ever since in the last two years and just honing in on little lyrics and changing them, so it’s really been awesome to see it change over the years." -- Taylor Swift

"Sparks Fly" received generally positive reviews by music critics, who praised it for its upbeat tempo. Others praised Taylor's lyrics of the song and have claimed that the song is a crossover between country and pop.

Following the release of "Speak Now", the song debuted at number 17 on the US Billboard Hot 100, due to strong digital sales. After the song was released as a single, it re-entered the US Billboard Hot 100 at #84. It peaked at number one at the US Billboard Hot Country Songs chart and was certified Platinum by the RIAA.

"Sparks Fly" was used as the opening song for the "[Speak Now World Tour](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/speak-now/speak-now-world-tour/ "Speak Now World Tour")". A music video for the song was released, featuring clips of various performances during the tour.

**"Dear John” is an ode to Taylor’s short-lived relationship with fellow singer-songwriter John Mayer. The two notably collaborated on Mayer’s 2010 song “[Half of My Heart,](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/features/half-of-my-heart/ "Half of My Heart")” which was released four months before “Dear John”.**

Taylor conveys her feelings of frustration over the way she was treated by John and how she disregarded the warnings from others. Besides the obvious song title, there are multiple references to Mayer directly, including the mention of their almost ten-year age gap. "The song "Dear John" is sort of like the last email you would ever send to someone that you used to be in a relationship with. Mayer, who is well-known for publicly talking about his relationships with various famous women in the press, has whined in an interview with _Rolling Stones_ about Taylor writing the song about him. In an issue of _Glamour_ magazine, Taylor called Mayer “presumptuous” for saying that he was “really humiliated” by the song’s lyrics. She went on to say that she did not want to hear his comments about the song, because of her desire to stay happy.

"I know it wasn’t good, so I don’t want to know. I put a high priority on staying happy, and I know what I can’t handle. It’s not that I’m this egomaniac and I don’t want to hear anything negative, because I do keep myself in check, but I’ve never developed that thick a skin. **"Enchanted" finds Taylor singing about meeting a guy she's attracted to without knowing if her instant infatuation is at all reciprocated. It was used as the theme song for Taylor's fragrances "[Wonderstruck](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/partnerships/elizabeth-arden/wonderstruck/ "Wonderstruck")" and "[Wonderstruck Enchanted](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/partnerships/elizabeth-arden/wonderstruck-enchanted/ "Wonderstruck Enchanted")".**

The power ballad was written by Taylor and produced by Nathan Chapman. Taylor wrote the song about a guy she met in New York City. She revealed the story behind the song in an interview:

"I had talked to him on email or something before, but I had never met him. And meeting him, it was this overwhelming feeling of: I really hope that you're not in love with somebody. And the whole entire way home, I remember the glittery New York City buildings passing by, and then just sitting there thinking, am I ever going to talk to this person again? And that pining away for a romance that may never even happen, but all you have is this hope that it could, and the fear that it never will. I started writing that in the hotel room when I got back. Because it just was this positive, wistful feeling of: I hope you understand just how much I loved meeting you. I hope that you know that meeting you was not something that I took lightly, or just in passing. And I think my favorite part of that song is the part where, in the bridge, it goes to sort of a stream of consciousness of 'Please don't be in love with someone else/Please don't have somebody waiting on you.' Because at that moment, that's exactly what my thoughts were. And it feels good to write exactly what your thoughts were in a certain moment." -- Taylor Swift

The guy in question had yet to hear the song at the time of the interview. However, Taylor added that she expects him to recognize that it's about their brief encounter when he does hear it as she threw in a certain word to give him a clue. "Using the word 'wonderstruck' was done on purpose," she explained (referring to the line "I'm wonderstruck, blushing all the way home"). Because that's a word which that person used one time in an email. And I don't think I've ever heard anybody use that term before, so I purposely wrote it in the song, so he would know."

The song describes Taylor's unrealized crush on Owl City's Adam Young and any lingering doubt about the mystery man's identity were removed when Young responded to the Country star's public serenade on his website. Addressing the singer in a 2011 Valentine's Day missive, he confessed that he too felt sparks fly when they first met. "You are a true princess from a dreamy fairy tale, and above all, I just want you to know," he wrote. "I was enchanted to meet you too." Adam also attached his own version of "Enchanted" featuring a new verse at the end, which was a direct response to Taylor's original lyrics.

"Speak Now" was not the original album title as at one point "Enchanted" was going to be the title track. Executive producer Scott Borchetta told _Billboard_: "We were at lunch, and she had played me a bunch of the new songs. I looked at her and I'm like, 'Taylor, this record isn't about fairy tales and high school anymore. That's not where you're at. I don't think the record should be called "Enchanted.'"

Not many songs can boast of having a perfume called after them, but this one does. Taylor teamed up with beauty company [_Elizabeth Arden_](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/partnerships/elizabeth-arden/ "Elizabeth Arden") for a scent called "Wonderstruck", which is named after a line in this tune. "I wrote the lyric, 'I'm wonderstruck, blushing all the way home,' for the song 'Enchanted' about the first time you meet someone," said the singer. "A fragrance can help shape someone's first impression and memory of you. It's exciting to think that 'Wonderstruck' will play a role in creating some of those memories."

"Ours" has been met positive reviews from critics praising Taylor's vocals, her songwriting, and her way to set the mood with the song.

The song appeared on the US iTunes Top 100 and debuted at number five on the Hot Digital Songs chart and #13 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The music video for the song was released in December 2011 and is the second video of Taylor's to be directed by Declan Whitebloom (after "Mean"), as well as the second video for which Taylor would do the concept for. The video received praise from music critics.

![Image 27](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=102x10000:format=png/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/iebb391da06ef7658/version/1548531157/image.png)

  

![Image 28](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=284x1024:format=jpg/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/i0b96a29e8fbe8d9f/version/1535922363/image.jpg)

**In “If This Was A Movie,” Taylor daydreams about a lost love coming back to her. It represented a more age-appropriate track for her then innocent "country hero" image.**

The fast-paced ballad suggests that the then 21-year-old Taylor had been through a breakup and wishes to reverse it: "I just want it back the way it was before/And I just wanna see you back at my front door," she sings.

Taylor was lyrically coming of age, abandoning the fantasy world of high school and exploring more mature content. A simple recurring guitar riff moves the song along, and its dramatic chorus features simple harmonies providing backup to Taylor's signature twang.

Taylor wrote the song with Martin Johnson, who is lead singer of Boys Like Girls. Previous collaborations between the pair include "[You'll Always Find Your Way Back Home](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/songs-written-for-other-artists/you-ll-always-find-your-way-back-home/ "You'll Always Find Your Way Back Home") " from the soundtrack of "[Hannah Montana: The Movie](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/videography/filmography/hannah-montana-the-movie/ "Hannah Montana: The Movie")" and the Boys Like Girls single "[Two Is Better Than One](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.jimdoweb.com/album-eras/features/two-is-better-than-one/ "Two Is Better Than One")."

The song is only available on the Deluxe Edition of "Speak Now" and was released as a promotional single in November, 2011.

"If This Was A Movie" received positivie reviews from music critics, with _Billboard_ rating it 4/5 stars.

As of 2018, Taylor has never performed the song live.

![Image 29](https://image.jimcdn.com/app/cms/image/transf/dimension=291x1024:format=jpg/path/s3628d4c0ebfcc161/image/ia6e8fa177187a394/version/1535922986/image.jpg)

**“Superman” is a track on the Deluxe Edition of "Speak Now." In the song, Taylor describes a boy who left her and hopes he will eventually come back to her when the time is right.**

Despite the sad premise, the melody and words are hopeful. Taylor wrote the track and produced in together with Nathan Chapman. She sang "Superman" for the first time during her solo acoustic segment at her September 24, 2011 concert in Kansas City. Before performing it, she explained:

"This is about, well, a guy, as usual. This was a guy that I was sort of enamored with. This song got its title by something that I just said randomly in conversation. \[When\] he walked out of the room, I turned to one of my friends and said, 'It's like watching Superman fly away.'" -- Taylor Swift

"Superman" was released as promotional single together with "If This Was A Movie" on  November 8, 2011.

In the movies, one of the primary rules of time travel is that you don’t do anything that could cause a tear in the space-time continuum. Plot lines that move between the past, present, and future emphasize the fragility of choice. Back in 2021, [Taylor Swift](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/how-taylor-swift-won-commentary-1235351833/) started building an alternate reality by dismantling her first six studio albums and repurposing them as part of an extensive re-recording process to regain ownership of her music. The question became, “What if we could do it all over again, even bigger?”

With the support of a fandom ready to ride to the ends of the earth with her, Swift stared down the barrel of boundless opportunity. She wasn’t the first artist to reclaim ownership of her songs by making them all over again, but she was the first to do it on such a monumental scale. It went beyond having a catalog full of era-defining records. Those songs became weapons in what she considers to be the fight of her life. In 2019, her former label Big Machine sold the master recordings of her first six studio albums to Scooter Braun, who later sold them to the private equity firm Shamrock Holdings. At the time, Swift couldn’t see that the circle would close with Shamrock [selling the albums back to her.](https://au.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/taylor-swift-buys-original-album-recordings-77575/) She only saw red.

“My musical legacy is about to lie in the hands of someone who tried to dismantle it,” Swift said when news of the [initial sale](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/taylor-swift-scooter-braun-big-machine-worst-case-scenario-853836/) broke in 2019. The re-recordings started as an elaborate mission to tank the stock of those songs and to show that their inherent value existed within her. She added the vault tracks. Then came “All Too Well (10 Minute Version) (Taylor’s Version).” Then, the [Eras Tour](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/the-eras-tour-taylor-swift-what-next-1235200483/) took it to explosive heights. In the end, Swift got her happy ending. She now owns every song she’s ever made. But the third act revelation is that her original recordings were always going to be better than their _Taylor’s Version_ counterparts. Every detail of those releases tells the story of the legacy she feared losing when her catalog fell into the hands of the wrong people. And every slight change made to them re-wrote her narrative.

Some of the changes were structural, but primarily strategic. When _Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_ arrived as the first release in the re-recording series, it came alongside “If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version), track five on _The More Fearless (Taylor’s Version) EP_. The original version was released two years after _Fearless_. With this project, Swift effectively reordered time by simply tinkering with the track list. As far as we know, the change didn’t cause any kind of multidimensional collapse. But still, this was different, and not insignificant for an artist who labors over the exact order in which songs appear on her albums. This was Taylor’s Version. It set the standard for what these albums could be. Swift could restructure, rearrange, and revise the past as she saw fit using perspective she didn’t gain until years after these original albums first arrived.

“If This Was a Movie” is the only song on _Speak Now (Deluxe Edition)_ that credits a co-writer, Boys Like Girls’ Martin Johnson. When _Speak Now_ (_Taylor’s Version)_ arrived, with the bonus track omitted, Swift shared: “I first made Speak Now, completely self-written, between the ages of 18 and 20.” In 2010, she wrote the record on her own to prove that no outside forces were responsible for her success. “The songs that came from this time in my life were marked by their brutal honesty, unfiltered diaristic confessions, and wild wistfulness,” she said. “It tells a tale of growing up, flailing, flying, and crashing … and living to speak about it.” And even though that singular credit never diminished her efforts, it was a loose end, so she tied it up.

For all her talk of brutal honesty and unfiltered confessions, Swift couldn’t help but clean things up as she went. The most notable change came on [“Better Than Revenge (Taylor’s Version).”](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/better-than-revenge-taylor-swift-speak-now-taylors-version-problematic-song-recording-1234732910/) The new version rewrites the lyric “She’s better known for the things that she does on the mattress,” which was generally tame for its time but fairly out of character for the country-pop sweetheart. It removes essential context for how Swift’s legacy is understood in regard to feminism and misogyny, an element of her narrative that has inspired multiple college-level gender studies courses. It might not be now, but at one point in time that was her truth.

On _Red (Taylor’s Version),_ Swift did the opposite. The 10-minute-version of “All Too Well” had so much more to say, not less. It remains disputed whether she actually wrote that “Fuck the patriarchy” line all those years ago, or whether it was the equivalent to replaying arguments with better comebacks long after they occurred. Was bringing the future to the past cheating? Maybe. Swift was making the rules up as she went. When Max Martin and some of the other _Red_ and _1989_ producers didn’t return, she re-produced their contributions herself with Christopher Rowe and Jack Antonoff. But like _Speak Now (Taylor’s Version),_ the perplexing production choices across the re-recordings largely buried the stormy emotion of the originals.

Love Music?
-----------

Get your daily dose of everything happening in Australian/New Zealand music and globally.

![Image 1](https://images-r2-2.thebrag.com/common/spinner.gif)

It could be argued that it doesn’t matter all that much. The original versions still exist, after all. Now, fans can make mix-and-match playlists combining their favorites. But up until Swift bought back her music, the understanding was that there wouldn’t be a need to go back to the originals. However, post-_Fearless_, as her sound became more complex, it became noticeably harder to recapture the moment with each re-release. Her voice has changed just as much as she has. No more faux-country twang. There’s a clear emotional detachment across her whole revised catalog, an expanse between the melodrama in her memories and the muted filter she views them through now.

As someone who routinely communicates with her fans through hidden clues and convoluted messages, Swift knows how much small, seemingly inconsequential details really do matter. She admitted as much when she revealed that, at the moment, she has less than 25 percent of _Reputation (Taylor’s Version)_ recorded. “The _Reputation_ album was so specific to that time in my life, and I kept hitting a stopping point when I tried to remake it,” she said. “It’s the one album in the first 6 that I thought couldn’t be improved upon by redoing it.” The snippet of [“Look What You Made Me Do (Taylor’s Version)”](https://youtu.be/nXlAUkd7zqE?si=qBQ_UC-5vs2mLW-F) that appeared in an episode of _The Handmaid’s Tale_ proves her point**.** It’s only a glimpse, but enough to justify needing a ouija board to contact the old Taylor. She’s the only one who could get it right.

There’s an indisputable specificity to the way Swift performs emotion across all of her albums. It’s obvious when she’s trying very hard and when she isn’t trying hard enough. You can hear it in the deepest grooves of those original records. You can feel its absence in the depths of the re-recordings. Swift’s biggest strength as a performer is that when she sings something, you’re inclined to believe her. It’s what made _Reputation_ so personal. The fact that, at that point in her career, she was having a really hard time getting people to believe her, was integral to the record. How does she access feeling like the most hated person on the planet again while being undoubtedly one of the most beloved? Why would she want to?

The Eras tour was the only place where the lines between the original recordings and Taylor’s Versions didn’t exist. The audience screamed back the songs that meant the most to them and it was all the same. Some might not have found Swift’s music until long after it was considered the ultimate betrayal to stream the “stolen versions,” as fans refer to them. The emotions that are old and jaded for her might be completely new to them. That’s their version. Others have lived with those words for years and know exactly what’s been missing when they’ve played the new versions in their cars and headphones.

In the movies, this is when the credits would roll and Swift would sing, “Nothing’s gonna change, not for me and you.” Which version do you hear?

_From [Rolling Stone US](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/taylor-swift-original-album-recordings-better-1235352886/)_

Taylor Swift Releases Bonus ‘Speak Now’ Songs on iTunes
=======================================================

[Cristin Maher](https://tasteofcountry.com/author/cristinmaher/)

[Cristin Maher](https://tasteofcountry.com/author/cristinmaher/)Published: November 13, 2011

*   [SHARE](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Ftasteofcountry.com%2Ftaylor-swift-bonus-speak-now-songs-itunes%2F%3Ftrackback%3Dfbshare_mobile "SHARE")

Up until recently, [Taylor Swift](https://tasteofcountry.com/tags/taylor-swift/) fans could only snag bonus tracks from 'Speak Now' if they bought the deluxe version of the album at their nearest Target store. However, Ms. Swift does not want to deprive her tech savvy fans of these songs for any longer, so the 21-year-old songstress has released the bonus tracks to iTunes.

If you have been dying to upload more Taylor Swift songs to your iPod, today is your lucky day! 'Ours,' 'If This Was a Movie,' and 'Superman' are now available for download on iTunes, as are acoustic renditions of 'Haunted' and 'Back to December.' The "Pop Mix" version of 'Mine' has also been added to the iTunes store.

Now that Swift has released these six bonus tracks to the World Wide Web, [Billboard](http://www.billboard.com/column/chartbeat/taylor-swift-set-for-multiple-debuts-on-1005512152.story#/column/chartbeat/taylor-swift-set-for-multiple-debuts-on-1005512152.story) is predicting that two of the songs -- 'Ours,' which Swift is releasing as her sixth 'Speak Now' single, and 'If This Was a Movie' -- may debut in the top 10 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Billboard explained their reasoning: "Her singles 'If This Was a Movie' and 'Ours' may sell around 150,000 and 130,000, respectively, by week's end on Sunday, Nov. 13, according to industry prognosticators." If Swift is able to achieve these numbers, these two songs could chart in the top 15 with a large possibility of both tracks charting in the top 10, as well.

If 'Ours' and 'If This Was a Movie' make their anticipated impact in the top 10 slots on Billboard's Hot 100 chart, they would mark Swift's first time back in the top 10 since October 2010, when 'Back to December' debuted at No. 6. If you want to download any of the new tracks, visit Taylor Swift's [artist page on iTunes](http://itunes.apple.com/us/artist/taylor-swift/id159260351?uo=4).

“60 MINUTES” PROFILE OF TAYLOR SWIFT TO AIR SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 20TH AT 7 PM ET / PT ON CBS

TAYLOR CELEBRATES 4TH CONSECUTIVE #1 SINGLE, THREE NEW BILLBOARD HOT 100 DEBUTS

NASHVILLE – November 16, 2011 – Four-time Grammy winner and Billboard’s 2011 Woman of the Year Taylor Swift will be profiled this Sunday, November 20th, on CBS News’ 60 Minutes. The segment includes concert and backstage footage from Taylor’s blockbuster Speak Now World Tour, and correspondent Lesley Stahl’s in-depth report offers viewers a candid conversation with Taylor, as well as a first-ever glimpse inside her Nashville condominium.  The full profile will be posted online at www.60minutes.com immediately after the show airs.

This week alone, Taylor sold more than 545,000 digital tracks. She debuted three new tracks (songs previously only available on the Target Deluxe Edition of Speak Now) on the all-genre Billboard Hot 100 singles chart, with “If This Was A Movie,” “Ours,” and “Superman,” entering the chart at numbers 10, 13 and 26, respectively. “Movie” marks Taylor’s Hot 100-record-extending eighth title to debut in the Top 10. She also locked down three of iTunes’ all-genre Top 10 spots, including positions #1 and #2, the day after the songs’ release.

Also this week, Taylor, who just last week was crowned Entertainer of the Year by the Country Music Association (for the second time), reached the #1 spot atop both the Billboard and Country Aircheck/Mediabase Country radio charts, with “Sparks Fly” becoming Taylor’s 4th consecutive #1 single from her 5 million plus-selling Speak Now album, and her 9th #1 song.

The 60 Minutes profile comes on the eve of the November 21st Big Machine Records release of SPEAK NOW WORLD TOUR – LIVE, CD / DVD combo-pak sets of the show. The North American leg of the tour wraps with sold-out shows at Madison Square Garden on November 21st and 22nd, and the tour has been extended into 2012 with shows in Australia and New Zealand.

"**If This Was a Movie**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") from the deluxe edition of her third studio album _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_ (2010). She wrote the track with [Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") and produced it with [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"). A fast-paced [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"), "If This Was a Movie" includes both acoustic and electric [string instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), drums, [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") notes, and full [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration"). In the lyrics, Swift's character begs an ex-lover to return to her and expects him to do so like it was a movie.

[Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") released "If This Was a Movie" digitally through the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") on November 8, 2011. The song reached charts in Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, where it debuted within the top ten of the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). Two publication reviews of the track were published in late 2011; one found it engaging, and the other deemed that it showcased newfound maturity within Swift's lyrics. Retrospective rankings of [Swift's songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_songs_by_Taylor_Swift "List of songs by Taylor Swift") have included the track within the lower-tier positions.

On March 17, 2023, Swift released a [re-recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_/(music/) "Re-recording (music)") of the song, titled "**If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)**", alongside three other songs to [streaming services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") in celebration of the start of her [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), where she debuted it live on piano during a [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") show on June 23. The re-recording was also part of an effort to re-record her early catalog after a [dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") over the ownership of the [master recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recordings "Master recordings").

Background and release
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

[![Image 2: Martin Johnson wearing a black outfit with an electric guitar smiling](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg/250px-Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg)

[Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") co-wrote "If This Was a Movie".

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") conceived her third studio album, _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_ (2010), as a collection of tracks about the things she had wanted to say but was unable to do with the people she had met.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Conger-1) There were as many as 25 songs Swift wrote for the album,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Conger-1) which she co-produced with [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Pastorek-2010-2) who had worked on her previous releases.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-3) By around mid-2010, she had secured the final track list,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-4) where all the tracks were written by her.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Pastorek-2010-2) One exception, however, was "If This Was a Movie", which Swift wrote with [Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") alongside other songs.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)

"If This Was a Movie" was included as a [bonus track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonus_track "Bonus track") in _Speak Now_'s deluxe edition,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-6) which was released as a [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation")\-exclusive alongside the standard edition on October 25, 2010.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-7) [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") made the song digitally available, along with the other bonus tracks, through the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") on November 8, 2011.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpencer2013106-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-9) On June 23, 2023, Swift debuted the track live on piano during a show in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), as part of her [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") (2023–2024).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-10)

Produced by Swift and Chapman,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) "If This Was a Movie" is a [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad") that critics described as "somber" and "sparkling".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Lane-2023-12) Set on a fast pace,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) it has a length of 5 minutes and 48 seconds.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-13) According to the _[Seattle Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Weekly "Seattle Weekly")_'s Erin Thompson, the song has a basic arrangement and structure, which he regarded as "[Swiftian](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Swiftian "wikt:Swiftian")".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) It features acoustic [string instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument") from [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), an electric guitar [amplified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_amplifier "Guitar amplifier") by [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_/(music/) "Distortion (music)"), and full [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) The [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") James E. Perone said that this arrangement could give "mixed-genre messages" to listeners.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) A simple, recurring guitar [riff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") is also played throughout,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) while drums and [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") notes lead Swift.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) The [verse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_/(music/) "Verse (music)")'s melody is performed at a low [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_register "Vocal register") and built on short [motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motif_/(music/) "Motif (music)") [figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_/(music/) "Figure (music)").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) The dramatic [chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5) where Swift sings with a [twang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twang "Twang") accompanied by [harmonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) [contrasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_/(music/) "Contrast (music)") the verse by being more melodious and performed at a higher register.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15)

In the lyrics, Swift's character pleads an ex-lover, who had left for six months, to come back to her, expecting him to do as such like it was a movie.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16) She imagines that through this perspective, he would be sorry to her for what mistake he made, and she would accept his apology and reconcile with him.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) A staff from _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_/(magazine/) "Billboard (magazine)")_ said that she was in a state of [coming of age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_of_age "Coming of age") in the lyrics, believing that she departs from the "fantasy world of high school" and examines "more mature content".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) Swift on the song often recalls the important memories when they were together.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5) It also includes a lyric about being in the rain ("Stand in the rain/'Til I came out"), which Thompson felt was used extensively in her songs.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-17)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) By the conclusion, the ideal ending does not happen like Swift had hoped for.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)

In late 2011, two publication reviews of "If This Was a Movie" were issued. Thompson included it in the _Seattle Weekly_'s "Nice Hits!"—a [column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column_/(periodical/) "Column (periodical)") that explores the best tracks out of the [top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_40 "Top 40") songs in a given time. He believed that while not "lyrically perfect", the track had the features that made Swift's songs engaging, including for what he considered vulnerable, relatable songwriting and a simple composition.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) _Billboard_'s staff stated that it showcased "a more age-appropriate track" from her.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11)

Over the years, retrospective rankings of [Swift's songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_songs_by_Taylor_Swift "List of songs by Taylor Swift") have included "If This Was a Movie" within the lower-tier positions. _[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_/(magazine/) "Paste (magazine)")_'s ranking, published in February 2020, listed the track as 115th among her 158 songs—one of its writers Jane Song took issue with the line, "Come back to me like", which she heard as "Come back to me, daylight".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-18) In her September 2020 ranking of Swift's 161 tracks for _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, Hannah Mylrea placed the song at 150th, writing that "it stutters towards the finish line" and that it was "frustratingly repetitive" overall.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-19) [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") listed the track as 266th in his October 2025 ranking of her 286 songs for _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-20) The next month, Nate Jones of _[Vulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_/(website/) "Vulture (website)")_ updated his ranking of Swift's 245 tracks, where the song was placed at 170th; he viewed it as "the [mirror image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_image "Mirror image")" of her track "[White Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "White Horse (Taylor Swift song)")" (2008) that, to him, made it "oddly superfluous".[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-21)

Carena Liptak of _[Taste of Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_of_Country "Taste of Country")_ included the song as 16th in her 2023 ranking of all 17 original tracks from _Speak Now_'s deluxe edition, saying that the song, while not among the album's most memorable, displayed "Swift's heartbreak songwriting at its wistful, [earworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earworm "Earworm")\-y best" and that its emotional impact was skillfully handled. She attributed the placement to how other tracks better showcase Swift's "ability to wax poetic on heartbreak and nostalgia".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-22)

After its digital release in November 2011, "If This Was a Movie" debuted at number ten on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart in the United States, where the track also reached number three on [Digital Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Song_Sales "Digital Song Sales") with 163,000 [downloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2011-23) The top-ten entry on the Hot 100 made the song become the fourth track from _Speak Now_ to do so, in addition to extending Swift's record of most top-ten debuts for any act with ten.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2011-23) It peaked atop on [Country Digital Song Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Digital_Song_Sales "Country Digital Song Sales") as well.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-USCDSS-24) Elsewhere, the song reached number 191 in the United Kingdom[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UK-25) and number 17 in Canada,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaHot100-26) where it also peaked at number 10 on Canada Digital Song Sales.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaDSS-27)

a Movie" (Taylor's Version)", on that day alongside three other songs to [streaming services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-30)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) The re-recording was also part of an Chapter_,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) which was also released on that day.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:2-33) Speculation ensued amongst fans regarding the song's release, according to some journalists, who questioned whether it would be featured on _Speak Now_'s re-recording, _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_/(Taylor%27s_Version/) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ When the album's track list was unveiled on June 5, 2023, the song was not on it.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Sager-2023-34)

"If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)" has a length of 3 minutes and 57 seconds.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-36) _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")_'s [Will Hodgkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Hodgkinson "Will Hodgkinson") described it as "straightforward, innocent, slightly breathy balladry with an orchestral backing".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16) The song was produced by Swift and its vocal engineer [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_/(record_producer/) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"). Musicians on the track were Amos Heller (who played bass), David Cook (piano), Matt Billingslea (drums and percussion), Max Bernstein (electric guitar), Mike Meadows (acoustic guitar), and Paul Sidoti (electric guitar); Bernstein also provided synthesizer [programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_/(music/) "Programming (music)"), while Meadows was the background vocalist. The [engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") were Bryce Bordone and Derek Garten, who was also the editor alongside Lowell Reynolds. David Payne was the recording engineer, assisted by Reynolds. The [mixer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_engineer "Mixing engineer") was [Serban Ghenea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serban_Ghenea "Serban Ghenea"), while the [mastering engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_engineer "Mastering engineer") was [Randy Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Merrill "Randy Merrill").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:2-33)

### Critical reception and chart performance

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Critical reception and chart performance")\]

In two reviews of the four songs that were released right before the start of Swift's Eras Tour, "If This Was a Movie" (Taylor's Version)" received favorable comments. Writing for _[The Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Freeman_/(newspaper/) "The Freeman (newspaper)")_, Januar Junior Aguja said that the track could have new fans because of Swift's vocals on the re-recording, claiming that they had improved.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) Hodgkinson wrote that the song was "corny but smart" and, to him, had Swift's early brilliance of "capturing an entire romantic drama in three minutes", considering that it had both an "[ingenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%A9nue "Ingénue") spirit" and professionally-written ruthlessness.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)

Commercially, "If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)" reached number two on the [Bubbling Under Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbling_Under_Hot_100 "Bubbling Under Hot 100")[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-USBUH100-37) and number four on Digital Songs in the US with 11,300 downloads.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2023-38) On Country Digital Song Sales, it became her record-extending 19th number-one entry and made "If This Was a Movie" the first song to have two versions peak atop the chart.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2023-38) On sales-component charts in other countries, the song reached number seven on Canada Digital Song Sales[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaDSS-27) and number thirteen on both [UK Singles Downloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Downloads_Chart "UK Singles Downloads Chart") and [UK Singles Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Sales_Chart "UK Singles Sales Chart").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UKDownloads-39)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UKSales-40) It also entered at number twelve on [Hot 40 Singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Aotearoa_Music_Charts#Hot_Singles_chart "Official Aotearoa Music Charts") in New Zealand.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-NZH40S-41)

Taylor Swift’s “If This Was a Movie” Sales Outpace “Ours” For Hot 100 Splash
============================================================================

  

by [**Brian Cantor**](https://headlineplanet.com/home/author/cantortainment/ "Posts by Brian Cantor") Nov 16, 2011, 3:42 pm

“Ours” might have received CMA Awards exposure as her next country single, but Taylor Swift’s “If This Was a Movie” will have the more impressive debut on tomorrow’s Hot 100 chart.

According to Billboard, “Movie” moved 162,000 downloads in its first week and will land at ten on the Overall Hot 100 chart. “Ours,” on sales of 148,000, will land at 13, still besting “Superman” (91,000 for 26).

All three singles, nonetheless, show Swift’s continued ability to move digital and physical copies of her music, even as the radio success of her mainstream singles slows. The three songs had previously been available on special deluxe editions of her “Speak Now” album but were not otherwise available for purchase until this past week.

Billboard notes that “Movie” gives Swift her eighth top 10 single debut, extending her pre-existing record. Lil Wayne, with six to his credit, is second.

Rihanna’s “We Found Love” will top the Hot 100 chart for its third consecutive week. It was also the top-selling digital record.

Taylor Swift Shares Four Unreleased Songs to Celebrate Start of 2023 Eras Tour
==============================================================================

By [Maxim Mower](https://holler.country/contributors/maxim-mower/)

As [Taylor Swift](https://holler.country/artists/taylor-swift) prepares to roll back the years with her new, [discography-encompassing Eras tour](https://holler.country/tours/taylor-swift-the-eras-tour), given the fact that she has almost 200 Billboard Hot 100 chart entries to her name, we suspect it's been more than a little tricky for the megastar to nail down her setlist.

The new tour is set to include much-loved throwbacks from albums such as _1989_, _Red_ and _Fearless_, along with fan-favourites from her most recent offering, _Midnights_.

However, Taylor has just made it even harder to decide which songs to leave out of her 2023 tour setlist, having today released four unreleased tracks.

These include ‘All Of The Girls You Loved Before’, which seems to have been taken from her _Lover_ sessions in 2019.

In addition to ‘All Of The Girls You Loved Before’, Taylor Swift has also released ‘Eyes Open (Taylor's Version)’, ‘If This Was A Movie (Taylor's Version)’ and ‘Safe & Sound (Taylor's Version)’.

The latter features Joy Williams and John Paul White, and the original rendition famously featured on _The Hunger Games_ soundtrack in 2012, as did ‘Eyes Open’.

The original recording of ‘If This Was A Movie (Taylor's Version)’ first featured on her widely acclaimed 2010 album, _Speak Now_.

It's one of the latest tracks to be revamped in light of Taylor Swift's quest to ensure she owns the masters to all her music.

It remains to be seen whether Taylor will be performing any of these during her 2023 _Eras_ run of shows, which kicks off tonight in Glendale, Arizona.

However, given the colossal amount of tracks she'll be choosing from, it seems likely these newly released songs are simply a gift to fans to help them celebrate the start of the tour.
